data.body:
Remediation epic: 3 closed, 6 in progress with changes pushed, 5 open. Stack of six on Gerrit: 2530 (F3), 2531 (F5), 2533 (F6), 2535 (F4), 2536 (F7), 2537 (F2).

TWO CI FAILURES, ONE CAUSE, AND ONE MISTAKE OF MINE.

2530 and 2531 both took Verified-1 with all four pytest jobs failing and lint passing. The jobs failed BEFORE pytest ran: `src/rebar file(s) over the 800-LOC hard cap` — `804 src/rebar/_commands/composer.py`. My F3 change added an import and expanded a comment on a file that was ALREADY SITTING AT EXACTLY 800. 2531 inherited it by stacking on F3. Note the module-size gate runs in CI but NOT in `make lint`, which is why local gates were green; four other files also sit at exactly 800, so this cap is tight repo-wide and any addition to those files breaks the build.

Then I compounded it: I trimmed composer.py and ran `git commit --amend` while HEAD was F4, folding an F3 fix into F4's commit — cross-ticket contamination. Unpicked it properly rather than leaving it: dropped composer.py out of F4's commit, amended F3 on its own branch (Change-Id preserved, re-pushed to 2530), then rebased F5/F6/F4 onto the corrected F3. Recommitting F4 minted a FRESH Change-Id, which opened duplicate change 2534; abandoned it with a comment explaining, and 2535 is the live one. That is exactly the duplicate-change hazard AGENTS.md warns about, caused by recommitting instead of amending.

F7 then hit the same wall from the other side: composer.py was back at exactly 800 and F7 needs to touch it. Rather than trimming someone else's code to make room, I moved the canonical tuple into rebar.types (which has room and already imports get_args after F3) and left composer consuming it on ONE line — net zero. Better shape anyway: every other consumer can now derive from the same export.

A UX detail worth recording: my first F7 attempt used tuple(sorted(get_args(TicketType))), which silently reordered the user-facing help line from the curated bug/epic/story/task to alphabetical. get_args preserves the Literal's DECLARATION order, so dropping sorted() keeps the help text byte-identical. Deriving a value is not automatically safe — the derivation has to preserve every fact the consumers rely on.

F2 was the same lesson, and the reviewer caught it before I wrote code: OPCERT_KINDS is an unordered frozenset while both copies are ordered tuples, and three consumers depend on that — argparse choices=, an API error message, and opcert_service.__all__ (so VALID_KINDS is PUBLIC API). tuple(sorted(...)) reproduces the exact existing order. A naive import of the frozenset would have changed a published type and made help output non-deterministic.

F4 grew slightly in scope: implementing it found a FOURTH copy of the blocking pair at _graph.py:256 that the finding did not name. Same file, same fact, same ticket, so fixed here.
